title: The effectiveness of various CSF diversion surgeries in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus: a systematic review and meta-analysis
article_subtype: Systematic review and meta-analysis of CSF diversion surgery outcomes
condition_or_topic: Effectiveness and safety of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) diversion surgery for idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH).
clinical_background: iNPH is a progressive condition involving gait disturbance, cognitive impairment and urinary incontinence alongside enlarged cerebral ventricles and normal CSF pressure. Its estimated prevalence is between 10 and 22 per 100,000. CSF shunting is considered the standard treatment, most commonly through ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting; lumboperitoneal (LP) and ventriculoatrial (VA) shunts are also used. Endoscopic third-ventriculostomy (ETV) has been proposed as an alternative, but its effectiveness is disputed. Reported surgical benefits and complication rates vary, and diagnosis and patient selection remain difficult because there is no definitive diagnostic test. Advances in diagnostic assessment and shunt technology, together with a growing body of studies, prompted an updated evaluation.
objectives: Estimate the effectiveness of CSF diversion procedures in patients with iNPH, using symptomatic improvement as the primary outcome.
Assess surgical complications and revision rates as secondary outcomes.
Evaluate the relative benefits and risks of the surgical techniques and whether their effectiveness has changed over time.
Explore whether clinical and methodological factors are associated with symptomatic improvement.
clinical_question: In patients with iNPH, how do VP, LP and VA shunting and ETV compare in symptomatic improvement, surgical complications and revision rates?
study_design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of original studies on CSF diversion surgery for iNPH, conducted according to Cochrane Collaboration and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance. Searches covered database inception through June 4, 2024, with additional manual searching. The review was registered in PROSPERO as CRD42023458526.

population.description: Patients with iNPH who underwent a clearly identified CSF diversion procedure; the pooled analysis included 4811 patients.
inclusion_criteria: Studies of patients with iNPH, or mixed hydrocephalus populations reporting iNPH results separately.
At least one symptom of Hakim’s triad: gait disturbance, cognitive impairment, or urinary incontinence, not explained by another neurological or non-neurological disease.
Radiological confirmation of ventriculomegaly with Evans index > 0.30.
Positive findings from an additional invasive diagnostic assessment based on CSF hydrodynamics, intracranial pressure, or CSF evacuation.
Assessment of disability, neurological morbidity, or Hakim’s triad symptoms at baseline and at least three months after surgery.
exclusion_criteria: Studies that did not clearly identify the surgical procedure.
Patients with secondary causes of normal-pressure hydrocephalus or neurological comorbidities that could affect shunt response.

comparators: Outcomes were stratified by CSF diversion procedure; the review did not establish a uniform direct head-to-head comparison.

primary: Symptomatic improvement after CSF diversion, defined by improvement on an outcome assessment scale between baseline and at least three months after surgery.

statistical_methods: Proportional meta-analyses estimated symptomatic improvement as the number of improved patients divided by sample size, separately by procedure; complications and revisions were also analysed. Random-effects models pooled estimates using inverse-variance weighting, with Hartung-Knapp adjustment of test statistics and confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed using the chi-squared statistic (I2), its associated p-value, and forest plots. Egger’s regression and asymmetry testing assessed publication bias (p < 0.05); trim-and-fill was planned if bias was detected. Meta-regressions examined baseline characteristics, iNPH disease measures, shunt details, and temporal trends. Influence analyses used leave-one-out estimates, Baujat plots, and influence diagnostics, with pooled analyses repeated after excluding identified outliers. Analyses used the ‘meta’ and ‘metafor’ packages in R software (version 4.3.2).
follow_up: Outcomes were assessed at baseline and at least three months after surgery. For studies reporting several follow-up periods, the period with the largest sample size was selected.
interpretation: Across 54 studies involving 4811 patients with iNPH, CSF diversion was associated with symptomatic improvement in 74% of patients. Improvement was greatest for gait, whereas cognitive and urinary symptoms improved in about half of patients. Estimated efficacy was similar across procedures, but heterogeneity and limited direct comparisons prevent a definitive ranking. Surgical success did not increase from 2005 to 2024 (p = 0.54), and complications and revisions remained clinically important. Higher preoperative mRS scores were associated with greater improvement after shunting; fixed-setting valves were associated with worse outcomes in LP shunt studies.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier reviews reported lower improvement rates, while a 2013 meta-analysis reported 71% efficacy, broadly consistent with the present finding of no improvement over time. Previous reports described early, sustained gait improvement in 64–77% of cases; the more variable cognitive response resembled findings from SINPHONI-2. Earlier iNPH studies reported complication rates up to 40%, compared with around 20% in this review, a rate the authors describe as consistent with the European multicentre iNPH study. Prior studies reported comparable effectiveness of LP and VP shunts, but this review cannot establish that either is superior. A 2017 study by Hung et al. reported fewer obstructions and revisions with VA than VP shunts and observed no cardiopulmonary complications; the authors state that updated evidence is needed to confirm that safety profile.
clinical_implications: The pooled improvement estimate can help communicate the potential likelihood of benefit from CSF diversion and serve as a benchmark for iNPH research.
Gait symptoms are more likely to improve than cognitive or urinary symptoms; improvement in the latter two domains is less consistent.
Similar pooled efficacy estimates do not establish equivalence between VP, LP, VA and ETV because direct comparative evidence is limited.
Adverse events may be severe. The review identified subdural collections and mechanical shunt problems as important complications, with mechanical problems contributing to reoperations.
The absence of improved success rates over time underscores the difficulty of identifying patients most likely to respond to shunting.
practice_implications: Base the choice among VP, LP and VA shunts on the surgeon’s expertise and the patient’s medical history and characteristics until stronger comparative evidence is available.
Consider VA shunting as an alternative when VP shunting is not feasible, such as in patients with abdominal adhesions.

Approach ETV outcomes cautiously: estimates come from small, heterogeneous samples, its revision rate is high, and the recent guidelines discussed by the authors do not recommend it because findings are inconsistent.
Treat shunt obstruction promptly; the authors note that approximately 75% of patients may subsequently improve symptomatically.
Improve the selection of candidates for CSF shunting; the authors identify advanced diagnostic techniques as a potential aid.
limitations: Substantial between-study heterogeneity affected pooled estimates. The authors relate this partly to the lack of a standardised iNPH outcome measure and consequent use of multiple scales.
Differences in criteria for shunt insertion, prognostic testing, valve types and antisiphon-device use complicated pooling.
Few randomised comparisons and sparse head-to-head data limited direct comparisons between CSF diversion procedures.
Most included studies were retrospective, although the authors found that study design did not significantly change the overall estimate.
Analyses used study-level rather than patient-level data, limiting the detail available.
ETV studies generally had small samples and were highly heterogeneous.
Too few included studies reported DESH for its predictive value to be assessed in this review.
strengths: The authors describe the review as the largest systematic review and meta-analysis to date of CSF diversion outcomes in iNPH, encompassing 54 studies and 4811 patients across the major procedures.
Eligibility criteria aligned with iNPH diagnostic consensus statements to strengthen the clinical relevance of pooled estimates.
Sensitivity analyses were used to examine heterogeneity; excluding identified outliers did not significantly alter the pooled effect.
open_questions: Which patients are most likely to benefit from CSF shunting, and how can they be identified more accurately?
Whether one CSF diversion procedure is preferable to another remains unresolved because comparative evidence is insufficient.
The adult complication profile of VA shunts requires more definitive, updated evidence.
The contribution of shunt dysfunction and progressive neurodegenerative disease to late deterioration remains poorly characterised.
future_directions: Develop better patient-selection criteria and investigate whether advanced diagnostic techniques improve identification of shunt responders.
Obtain stronger direct comparative evidence on the outcomes of CSF diversion procedures.
Investigate VA shunt complications in more definitive, updated adult studies.
Use patient-level data to provide more detailed insight into surgical outcomes.

main_findings.description: Symptomatic improvement after any CSF diversion procedure in patients with iNPH
main_findings.context: The analysis included 54 studies and 4811 patients. Improvement was assessed with a scale before and after surgery.
The Summary gives the confidence interval as 70–79%, whereas the Results give 70–78%.
The confidence intervals for the procedure-specific estimates overlapped; the authors did not identify a clearly superior procedure.

main_findings.description: Improvement in urinary symptoms after CSF diversion
Surgical success showed no significant overall change by study year
main_findings.context: The analysis covered 2005 to 2024. The Results also report p = 0.54 for the absence of an overall temporal trend.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: Among 4099 patients in 41 studies assessing complications, the overall surgical complication rate was 20.6%. The composite included subdural collections, clinical overdrainage without radiological changes, infection, intracerebral haemorrhage or ischaemic events, shunt malfunction, and mortality.
safety_results.related_deaths: Mortality attributed to CSF diversion surgery was 0.2% (n = 9).
notable_adverse_events: Subdural collections occurred in 7.3% (n = 297). Among these collections, 61.3% were subdural haematomas, 19.8% were subdural hygromas, and 18.9% were unspecified.
Shunt malfunction occurred in 6.0% of cases (n = 246); obstruction accounted for 69.1% of malfunctions.
Clinical overdrainage without radiological changes occurred in 3.6% of cases (n = 147).
The overall infection rate was approximately 2% (n = 70).
Haemorrhagic and ischaemic events occurred in less than 1% of patients (n = 36).
The pooled complication rate after VP shunting was 20% (95% CI: 16–24%).
The pooled complication rate after LP shunting was 25% (95% CI: 15–39%).
The pooled complication rate after ETV was 6% (95% CI: 3–11%).

A complication meta-analysis for VA shunts was not performed because fewer than n < 3 studies reported complications. The authors found no notable differences in complication profiles between procedures.

subgroup_analyses: Across VP, LP, and VA shunts, gait improvement ranged from 67 to 74%, cognitive improvement from 49 to 59%, and improvement in urinary symptoms from 50 to 56%.

After shunt surgery, studies with follow-up of less than 12 months reported improvement of 70% (95% CI 61–77%); those with follow-up of 12 months or more but less than or equal to 24 months reported 75% (95% CI: 69–80%); and those with follow-up beyond 24 months reported 76% (95% CI: 72–80%).
Prospective studies alone yielded an estimated success rate of 76% (95% CI: 69–82%), compared with 74% (95% CI: 69–79%) for retrospective studies alone; the difference was not significant (p = 0.53).
Procedure-specific temporal analyses found no significant relationship between study year and success for VP, LPS, or ETV. VA showed a negative temporal trend.
Study quality measured by NOS did not significantly affect the effect size (p = 0.70). Excluding studies identified as outliers did not significantly change the pooled effect.

In meta-regression, a higher preoperative mRS score predicted greater overall shunt improvement: coefficient 1.2987 (0.4837), p = 0.0250. The Results also describe an overall coefficient of 1.3 (p = 0.025). For LPS, the coefficient was 2.1376 (0.5267), p = 0.0457; the Results also describe this coefficient as 2.
For LPS, the shunt valve type meta-regression coefficient was −3.2558 (1.2413), p = 0.0394. The Results describe a fixed-setting valve as a negative predictor and give p = 0.03.

secondary_results: Surgical revision was assessed in 34 studies. The Results report revisions in 15.2% of cases (389 out of 2565 cases), whereas the Summary reports a revision rate of 15.1%.

The pooled surgical revision rate after ETV was 23% (95% CI: 10–46%); after VP shunting it was 12% (95% CI: 8–17%). A revision meta-analysis for VA shunts was not performed because fewer than n < 3 studies reported revisions.
Of 1963 studies screened, 54 were included, comprising 4811 patients. Of the included studies, 53 were judged to have low risk of bias or some concern, and one had high risk.

The overall Egger’s asymmetry assessment did not identify significant publication bias (p = 0.18); the figure reports p = 0.1761. The Results state that the absence of significant publication bias also held across the individual CSF diversion procedures.

document_sections.heading: Summary
document_sections.content: The summary presents the clinical rationale, methods, principal findings and interpretation in its Background, Methods, Findings and Interpretation subsections.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is commonly managed by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) diversion, predominantly ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting, but also lumboperitoneal (LP) and ventriculoatrial (VA) shunting and endoscopic third-ventriculostomy (ETV). Despite widespread use of these operations and advances in diagnosis, current evidence on surgical outcomes is limited.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The authors systematically reviewed and meta-analysed CSF diversion in iNPH. Symptomatic improvement was the primary efficacy outcome; surgical complications were secondary outcomes. Searches covered original studies from database inception through June 4, 2024. Analyses used random-effects meta-analysis, meta-regression and influence assessment. The registration identifier was CRD42023458526.

document_sections.heading: Findings
document_sections.content: Of 1963 screened studies, 54 were included, contributing 4811 patients. More than 74% improved after surgery (95% CI: 70–78%). Reported efficacy was 75% for VP shunting (95% CI 70–79%), 75% for VA shunting (95% CI: 70–80%), 70% for LP shunting (95% CI: 52–83%) and 69% for ETV (95% CI: 58–78%). Gait improved in 72% (95% CI: 67–77%); urinary and cognitive dysfunction each improved in approximately 50%. Efficacy did not increase from 2005 to 2024 (p = 0.54). Complications affected 20.6% of cases, and the summary reports a surgery revision rate of 15.1%.

document_sections.heading: Interpretation
document_sections.content: Across 2005 to 2024, the authors found no improvement in overall CSF diversion efficacy; 74% of cases improved. No operation was clearly superior. Urinary and cognitive symptoms improved in only about half of patients. Unchanged efficacy and frequent complications underscore the need for better selection of patients most likely to benefit from CSF shunting.

document_sections.heading: Research in context
document_sections.content: This section places the analysis alongside earlier reviews and describes its contribution and clinical implications.

document_sections.heading: Evidence before this study
document_sections.content: iNPH is progressive and considered potentially reversible with CSF shunting, but reported efficacy and complication rates vary, partly with patient selection. The authors searched PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews through June 4th, 2024, for meta-analyses concerning iNPH surgery and CSF shunts. They identified two: one concentrated on VP shunts, while limited data constrained the other's assessment of ETV. Outcomes differed substantially, and the earlier evidence extended only to 2017. Subsequent developments in invasive diagnostic tools, consensus criteria and shunt technology warranted an updated assessment, including changes in efficacy over time.

document_sections.heading: Added value of this study
document_sections.content: This review pooled data from 4811 patients with iNPH. Improvement across CSF diversion operations was consistently 74%, without evidence that a particular procedure was superior. Gait generally improved, while complications occurred at a moderate frequency. Success rates had not improved over the preceding 19 years, reinforcing the need for better patient selection.

document_sections.heading: Implications of all the available evidence
document_sections.content: The authors consider the analysis an update of clinical efficacy and its temporal pattern. CSF shunt procedures can reverse iNPH symptoms, but complications can be severe and require careful consideration. Persistently unchanged efficacy points to difficulty identifying patients likely to respond; addressing that difficulty may require advanced diagnostic techniques.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: iNPH is a progressive syndrome involving gait disturbance, cognitive impairment and urinary incontinence alongside ventricular enlargement despite normal CSF pressure. Estimated prevalence is between 10 and 22 per 100,000 and is substantially higher in certain vulnerable groups, including residents of extended-care facilities. CSF shunts are regarded as the gold-standard treatment. VP shunts are widely preferred; LP shunts are used substantially in some regions, whereas VA shunts are less common. ETV has been proposed as an alternative involving systolic CSF outflow into the subarachnoid space, but its efficacy is disputed. Despite advances in imaging and CSF-dynamics assessment, the size of the treatment benefit remains uncertain because reported success varies. Shunting can cause important complications, including infection and intracranial haematoma, whose reported frequencies differ. Diagnosis lacks a definitive test. The 2021 Japanese guidelines and 2005 American–European guidelines differ on age restrictions and thresholds used to distinguish iNPH from other neurodegenerative diseases; variation in their interpretation may affect surgical eligibility and study outcomes. Expanding evidence on shunts and, to a lesser extent, ETV permits reassessment. Advances in clinical and radiological selection may improve identification of likely responders; recent consensus guidance favours a more nuanced diagnostic algorithm and CSF biomarkers for outcome prediction. The authors therefore aimed to update estimates of the relative benefits and risks of CSF diversion and assess temporal efficacy trends.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis under Cochrane Collaboration and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance, registered as CRD42023458526. The following subsections specify search, eligibility, extraction, quality assessment and analysis.

document_sections.heading: Literature search
document_sections.content: MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library of Registered Clinical Trials and World Health Organisation International Clinical Trials Registry Platform were searched from inception to June 4, 2024. Search concepts covered iNPH and surgery, shunting or named CSF diversion procedures. Manual searches yielded additional articles.

document_sections.heading: Study inclusion and exclusion criteria
document_sections.content: Abstract screening required an iNPH population, or a mixed-hydrocephalus population with separately analysable iNPH cases, and CSF diversion surgery. Paediatric hydrocephalus, non-English publications, conference abstracts, case reports and case series (n < 5) were excluded. Full-text screening applied the specified diagnostic and outcome criteria. The study-selection flow is shown in Fig. 1.

document_sections.heading: iNPH diagnostic criteria
document_sections.content: Eligible studies required at least one feature of Hakim’s triad—gait disturbance, cognitive impairment or urinary incontinence—unexplained by other neurological or non-neurological conditions; a mean study age >60 years; radiologically confirmed ventriculomegaly with Evans index > 0.30; and positive additional invasive testing based on CSF hydrodynamics, intracranial pressure or CSF removal. Examples were CSF tap testing, extended lumbar drainage, infusion testing and intracranial pressure monitoring.

document_sections.heading: Outcome measures
document_sections.content: The primary endpoint was improvement on an assessment scale measured before surgery and at least three months afterward in every patient; the scale had to assess disability, neurological morbidity or Hakim’s triad symptoms. Secondary endpoints were surgical complications and revision rates. Studies were excluded when the operation was insufficiently specified or when secondary normal-pressure hydrocephalus or neurological comorbidity could affect shunt response. Authors were contacted about missing data.

document_sections.heading: Eligibility assessment and data extraction
document_sections.content: References were managed and deduplicated in Covidence. Three reviewers assessed eligibility, with disagreements resolved through discussion with an independent reviewer. Covidence was also used to extract design, surgical patient counts, methods, diagnostic criteria, follow-up, definitions and assessments of improvement, and complications. For studies reporting several follow-up points, the authors selected the period retaining the largest sample and least loss to follow-up. Multiple reports of one study were linked.

document_sections.heading: Quality assessment and data analysis
document_sections.content: Three independent reviewers assessed studies with an adapted Newcastle–Ottawa Score (NOS), resolving assessments with an independent reviewer. Selection, comparability and outcome contributed to an overall score out of 9; bias was classified as high, with some concern or low. Egger’s regression and asymmetry testing assessed publication bias, with p < 0.05 considered significant; detected bias would prompt trim-and-fill estimation. For each procedure, improvement was the number of improved patients divided by sample size. Complications and revisions were analysed separately. Random-effects models addressed anticipated heterogeneity, inverse-variance weighting pooled effects, and the Hartung-Knapp method adjusted statistics and confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed with I2 and its p-value and by examining forest plots. Meta-regressions related responder proportions to available baseline, disease and shunt characteristics selected according to expert opinion and data availability; variance estimation was kept consistent with the meta-analyses. Leave-one-out influence assessments generated Baujat plots, diagnostics and pooled estimates, and analyses were repeated without identified outliers. Preparation, analysis and forest plots used the ‘meta’ and ‘metafor’ packages in R version 4.3.2.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: Among 1963 reviewed studies, 54 papers met inclusion criteria, yielding 4811 patients with iNPH. On the modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, 53 studies had low bias or some concern and one had high risk. The overall Egger test did not indicate significant publication bias (p = 0.18), nor did procedure-specific assessments. Fig. 2 reports an asymmetry analysis of n = 41 data points with p = 0.1761; its funnel plot depicts n = 54 included studies.

document_sections.heading: Study type and design
document_sections.content: Three (5.6%) studies were randomised parallel trials, 19 (35.1%) were prospective, and 32 (59.3%) were retrospective. The most frequent study origins were Germany (14.8%), Japan (13.0%) and the United States of America (11.1%). VP shunting alone was studied in 35 studies (n = 2442), LP alone in 7 (n = 333), VA alone in 3 (n = 152), and ETV alone in 5 (n = 159). Another 4 studies compared procedures among 1725 patients: 906 received VP, 636 LP, 167 VA and 16 ETV. Of 49 shunt studies, 29 used programmable valves, 6 fixed valves, 7 both types and 7 did not specify valve type. The most common valves were Codman Hakim adjustable valve (Codman) (24.8%), Strata (Medtronic) (12.1%) and proGAV (Miethke and Aesculap) (11.9%). Fig. 2 maps publication origins for n = 53 studies, excluding a European multicentre study; one investigation took place in 2 countries, Sweden and Norway. Its country counts are Germany (n = 8), Japan (n = 7), United States of America (n = 6), Italy (n = 5), China (n = 5), Sweden (n = 4), Brazil (n = 4), Norway (n = 2), and one each from the United Kingdom, The Netherlands, Spain, Austria, Denmark, South Korea, India, Greece, Finland, Egypt, the Czech Republic, Australia and Turkey. Table 1 describes included studies’ designs, diagnostic and response criteria, operations and follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Patient characteristics
document_sections.content: Mean age was 72 years, and 40.9% were female. Gait abnormalities were present in 90.2%, cognitive impairment in 71.2% and urinary symptoms in 73.7%; 64.1% had every component of Hakim’s triad. Mean symptom duration was 23.3 months. Preoperative and postoperative assessments included iNPH grading scale (14 studies), Mini-Mental State Examination (14 studies), modified Rankin Scale (13 studies), Japanese iNPH grading scale (11 studies), Kiefer scale score (6 studies), Black grading scale (4 studies), timed up and go test (4), quality of life assessment (4 studies) and Tinetti test score (3 studies).

document_sections.heading: Meta-analysis Symptom improvement
document_sections.content: Improvement on a preoperative-to-postoperative scoring scale occurred in 74% across CSF diversion procedures (95% CI: 70–78%). Procedure-specific estimates were 75% after VP shunting (95% CI: 70–78%), 75% after VA shunting (95% CI: 70–80%), 70% after LP shunting (95% CI: 52–83%) and 69% after ETV (95% CI: 58–78%). Overlapping confidence intervals did not indicate a difference between pooled estimates. Gait improved in 72% (95% CI: 67–77%), cognition in 55% (95% CI: 46–65%) and urinary symptoms in 54% (95% CI: 45–63%). Across VP, LP and VA shunts, gait improvement ranged from 67 to 74%, cognitive improvement from 49 to 59%, and urinary improvement from 50 to 56%. After shunting, improvement was 70% (95% CI 61–77%) with follow-up of less than 12 months, 75% (95% CI: 69–80%) with follow-up of 12 months or more but no more than 24 months, and 76% (95% CI: 72–80%) beyond 24 months. Figs. 3–5 display procedure-, symptom- and follow-up-stratified forest plots.

document_sections.heading: Complication profile
document_sections.content: Complications were assessed in 41 studies. The combined endpoint comprised subdural collections, symptomatic overdrainage without imaging changes, infections, intracerebral haemorrhage or ischaemia, shunt malfunction and death. Among 4099 patients, overall complications occurred in 20.6%. Subdural collections affected 7.3% (n = 297), and malfunction affected 6.0% (n = 246). Of subdural collections, 61.3% were haematomas, 19.8% hygromas and 18.9% unspecified. Obstruction constituted 69.1% of malfunctions. Clinical overdrainage without radiological change, such as positional headache, occurred in 3.6% (n = 147). Infection affected approximately 2% (n = 70); haemorrhagic and ischaemic events occurred in less than 1% (n = 36). Surgery-related mortality was 0.2% (n = 9). Complication estimates were 20% after VP shunting (95% CI: 16–24%), 25% after LP shunting (95% CI: 15–39%) and 6% after ETV (95% CI: 3–11%). VA complication meta-analysis was not performed because reporting studies were insufficient (n < 3). The authors found no notable differences in complication profiles between procedures. Fig. 6 displays procedure-specific complication data.

document_sections.heading: Revision surgeries
document_sections.content: Revision after initial diversion was investigated by 34 studies. Reoperation was required in 15.2% (389 out of 2565 cases). The revision estimate was 23% for ETV (95% CI: 10–46%) and 12% for VP shunting (95% CI: 8–17%). VA revision data were insufficient for meta-analysis (n < 3). Fig. 7 depicts revisions by procedure.

document_sections.heading: Meta-regression analysis
document_sections.content: Table 2 presents separate meta-regressions of clinical and procedural predictors against the proportion improving. Higher preoperative modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores predicted greater improvement overall, with a coefficient described in the prose as 1.3 (p = 0.025), and in LP shunt studies, with a coefficient described as 2. The table gives the overall coefficient as 1.2987 (0.4837) [0.0250]* and the LP coefficient as 2.1376 (0.5267) [0.0457]*. Fixed-setting valve use was described as a significant negative predictor (p = 0.03); the table reports an LP shunt valve-type coefficient of −3.2558 (1.2413) [0.0394]*.

document_sections.heading: Temporal and sensitivity analysis
document_sections.content: Across publication years 2005 to 2024, surgical success showed no clear temporal trend (p = 0.54). Fig. 8 gives a mixed-effects meta-regression coefficient of 0.0023 and p-value = 0.5420. Procedure-specific analyses found no significant temporal association for VP, LPS or ETV, whereas VA showed a negative trend in success over time. NOS study quality did not significantly affect effect size (p = 0.70). Prospective studies yielded 76% success (95% CI: 69–82%), compared with 74% for retrospective studies (95% CI: 69–79%); the estimates did not differ significantly (p = 0.53). Removing influence-analysis outliers did not materially change effect size.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content:
The authors describe this as the largest review and meta-analysis to date of CSF diversion outcomes in iNPH, covering 54 studies and 4811 patients. Improvement was frequent but had not risen over the last 19 years. Although procedures had similar pooled efficacy, between-study heterogeneity and few direct comparisons prevent firm comparative conclusions. Overall improvement of 74% at follow-up may inform discussions of treatment success and serve as a research benchmark. Earlier reviews reported lower improvement. The authors attribute some historical variation to early descriptions emphasising striking reversals and to patient selection complicated by overlap with neurodegenerative conditions that do not respond to shunting. Their consensus-aligned eligibility criteria sought to strengthen the pooled estimates.

Gait ataxia improved more consistently than cognition or urinary symptoms. Earlier reports described early, sustained gait improvement in 64–77% of cases. Cognitive improvement in this analysis was around 50%, resembling findings of the Study of Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus on Neurological Improvement 2 (SINPHONI-2) trial. The authors suggest gait may respond to mechanical CSF decompression because its relevant frontal subcortical and periventricular pathways are affected by ventricular enlargement. Cognition involves wider networks, including the hippocampus, and may overlap with shunt-unresponsive dementias. Urinary symptoms improved in about half of patients; the authors propose that pressure normalisation in periventricular bladder-control pathways may contribute, while extensive control networks and concomitant neurodegeneration may limit recovery.

Sustained improvement at longer follow-up contrasted with previous reports of waning long-term benefit. The authors suggest that large tertiary centres and stringent follow-up may partly explain this pattern. Nevertheless, up to 20% deteriorate several years after initial benefit and are termed ‘late shunt non-responders’; shunt dysfunction and advancing neurodegeneration are proposed contributors, although this phenomenon remains poorly characterised. Adjustable valves can permit CSF-flow titration and address deterioration in some patients.

Across operations, improvement was generally around 69–75%, with overlapping confidence intervals, but direct comparative studies were insufficient. Guidelines since the first description of normal-pressure hydrocephalus in 1965 have supported CSF shunting without specifying an operation. VP remains the most common procedure worldwide. LP shunts, historically less favoured because of failure and overdrainage, are more common in Japan and elsewhere to reduce intracranial risks. Earlier studies reported LP safety and non-inferior efficacy relative to VP; the authors' results do not support definitively preferring either. Comparisons may be influenced by geography, diagnostic thresholds, younger average ages in European studies, and differing obesity and cardiovascular comorbidity burdens. VA shunts place the distal catheter in the right cardiac atrium and may shorten surgery, but are generally considered when VP is not feasible, including with abdominal adhesions. Concern about serious haematological and cardiopulmonary events largely derives from paediatric evidence, with limited adult data. Hung et al. reported in 2017 that VA significantly reduced obstruction and revision relative to VP among iNPH patients and observed no cardiopulmonary events; confirmation in more definitive, updated studies is needed. Pending such evidence, the authors favour choosing a shunt according to local expertise and patient characteristics.

ETV creates an opening in the third-ventricle floor for CSF flow toward basal cisterns. Its iNPH evidence requires caution because samples were generally small, apart from Gangemi et al., and heterogeneous. Recent guidelines do not recommend ETV because findings are inconsistent. This analysis found modest improvement with a wide confidence interval and a high revision rate. Anatomical eligibility can also be limited by magnetic resonance imaging findings.

Adverse events can be severe. Subdural haematomas and hygromas range from incidental imaging findings to emergencies. Earlier evidence indicates most subdural haematomas resolve spontaneously after valve-pressure increases, with only 10% requiring evacuation. The authors found mechanical problems, including obstruction and migration, to be frequent contributors to reoperation. Prompt treatment of obstruction matters because approximately 75% of affected patients can subsequently improve symptomatically. Early iNPH studies reported complications up to 40%; this review found a significantly lower rate around 20%, consistent with the European multicentre iNPH study. The authors relate the reduction to better operations, gravitational control devices and antibiotic protocols. Previous evidence indicates adjustable valves halve subdural collections relative to fixed-pressure valves, supporting their greater cost.

Despite initial consensus guidelines in 2005, this review found no significant rise in surgical success through 2024; a 2013 meta-analysis reported a similar efficacy of 71%. The authors suggest diagnostic difficulty in identifying shunt-responsive patients may contribute. Extended lumbar drainage and intracranial pressure monitoring have been reported to identify responders reliably, though operator and centre effects may occur; their replication suggests potential diagnostic value. In this study, greater baseline neurological morbidity measured by mRS predicted greater improvement, possibly because more severe symptoms make response easier to classify. Fixed valves were associated with worse LP outcomes; the authors suggest gravity and position may make valve settings more consequential for LP than VP. Disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH) has been reported to predict shunt response, but too few included studies reported DESH for this analysis.

Declared limitations are substantial between-study heterogeneity with high I2 values, lack of a standard iNPH outcome measure requiring multiple scales, differences in surgical eligibility, prognostic testing, valves and antisiphon devices, few randomised interprocedural trials, a predominantly retrospective evidence base, and study-level rather than patient-level data. Sensitivity analyses were used to address heterogeneity, and retrospective design did not affect the overall estimate. The authors conclude that improvement is consistently high across procedures, while heterogeneity complicates evaluation. They support selecting among VP, LP and VA according to surgeon preference and medical history, and identify better patient selection and potentially advanced diagnostic methods as research and clinical priorities after two decades of unchanged success.

tables.summary: The table describes each included study’s setting, design, procedure, population, diagnostic and response criteria, assessment instruments, follow-up, and reported mean age. Its diagnostic thresholds and outcome definitions vary across studies.

tables.title: Table 2: Meta-regression analyses
tables.summary: Separate meta-regressions relate each predictor to the proportion improving after surgery. Higher preoperative mRS scores had significant positive associations for LPS and Overall Shunt; the LPS shunt-valve-type coefficient was significant and negative. Parenthesised figures are identified as 95% confidence intervals, and bracketed figures with an asterisk indicate reported significant p-values. N/A denotes insufficient reporting by n < 3 studies.

main_conclusion: CSF diversion was associated with symptom improvement in a substantial proportion of patients with iNPH, without evidence that one procedure was clearly superior or that efficacy improved from 2005 to 2024. The authors favour choosing among VP, LP, and VA shunts according to patient history and surgical expertise, while emphasising complications and the need for better selection of likely responders.
narrative_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed symptomatic outcomes and complications after CSF diversion for iNPH. It included 54 studies and 4811 patients, covering VP, LP, and VA shunts and ETV. Across procedures, 74% improved (95% CI: 70–78%). Improvement was reported in 75% after VP shunting (95% CI: 70–78%), 75% after VA shunting (95% CI: 70–80%), 70% after LP shunting (95% CI: 52–83%), and 69% after ETV (95% CI: 58–78%). Overlapping confidence intervals and limited direct comparisons did not establish a superior procedure. Gait improved in 72% (95% CI: 67–77%); cognitive and urinary symptoms improved in 55% (95% CI: 46–65%) and 54% (95% CI: 45–63%), respectively. Among 4099 patients evaluated for complications, the overall rate was 20.6%; subdural collections occurred in 7.3% and shunt malfunction in 6.0%. Surgical revision was required in 15.2% of cases assessed for that outcome. Overall surgical efficacy showed no significant temporal change from 2005 to 2024 (p = 0.54). The authors note substantial between-study heterogeneity, differing outcome measures, and few randomised head-to-head comparisons. They consider patient selection central to improving results; until stronger comparative evidence is available, they support basing the choice among VP, LP, and VA shunts on patient characteristics and local surgical expertise. Recent guidelines do not recommend ETV because findings have been inconsistent.
